RichTextView-module-scss-module__IzrXdG__richTextViewContainer RichTextView-module-scss-module__IzrXdG__clamped"><p>We are seeking a dedicated and experienced Abattoir Supervisor to oversee daily operations within our meat processing facility. In this role, you will be responsible for ensuring that all slaughter and processing activities are conducted efficiently, safely, and in compliance with regulatory standards. You will lead a team of processing staff, manage production schedules, and maintain high standards of quality and hygiene. The ideal candidate will have a strong background in meat processing, excellent leadership skills, and a commitment to workplace safety. This is a contract internship position based in Bottineau, ND, offering a unique opportunity to gain hands-on supervisory experience in the accounting industry's food processing sector. If you are a proactive problem-solver with a passion for operational excellence, we encourage you to apply.</p><p><strong>Responsibilities</strong></p><ol><li data-list="bullet">Supervise and coordinate the daily activities of abattoir staff, including scheduling, task assignment, and performance monitoring to ensure optimal productivity.</li><li data-list="bullet">Ensure compliance with all local, state, and federal regulations regarding animal welfare, food safety, and workplace safety, including USDA and OSHA standards.</li><li data-list="bullet">Oversee the slaughter and processing of animals, ensuring that all procedures are performed humanely and in accordance with industry best practices.</li><li data-list="bullet">Maintain accurate records of production volumes, yields, and inventory, and prepare reports for management review.</li><li data-list="bullet">Conduct regular inspections of equipment and facilities to ensure they are clean, well-maintained, and operating efficiently.</li><li data-list="bullet">Train new employees on proper handling techniques, safety protocols, and sanitation procedures.</li><li data-list="bullet">Collaborate with quality assurance and maintenance teams to address any issues and implement continuous improvement initiatives.</li><li data-list="bullet">Manage inventory of supplies and coordinate with procurement to ensure timely availability of necessary materials.</li><li data-list="bullet">Investigate and resolve any operational issues or employee concerns in a timely and professional manner.</li><li data-list="bullet">Promote a culture of safety and teamwork, leading by example and enforcing all company policies.</li></ol><p><strong>Requirements</strong></p><ol><li data-list="bullet">Minimum of 4 years of experience in an abattoir or meat processing environment, with at least 1 year in a supervisory or leadership role.</li><li data-list="bullet">In-depth knowledge of meat processing techniques, animal handling, and food safety regulations (e.g., HACCP, USDA).</li><li data-list="bullet">Strong leadership and team management skills, with the ability to motivate and develop staff.</li><li data-list="bullet">Excellent organizational and problem-solving abilities, with a keen attention to detail.</li><li data-list="bullet">Effective communication skills, both verbal and written, to interact with staff, management, and regulatory officials.</li><li data-list="bullet">Ability to work in a fast-paced, physically demanding environment, including exposure to cold temperatures and loud noises.</li><li data-list="bullet">Certification in food safety or animal welfare is preferred (e.g., HACCP certification).</li><li data-list="bullet">Basic computer skills for record-keeping and reporting; experience with inventory management software is a plus.</li><li data-list="bullet">Flexibility to work various shifts, including weekends and holidays, as needed.</li><li data-list="bullet">High school diploma or equivalent; additional technical or vocational training in meat processing or related field is advantageous.</li></ol></div></span></div><div </p><p><strong>Job Title:</strong> Principal Autonomous Systems Engineer</p> <p><strong>Location:</strong> New York, New York, United States</p> <p><strong>Salary:</strong> $285000 - $320000</p> <p><strong>Job Summary:</strong> We are seeking a highly skilled and experienced Principal Autonomous Systems Engineer to join our dynamic team. As a Principal Autonomous Systems Engineer, you will play a crucial role in developing, implementing, and maintaining cutting-edge autonomous systems for our company. You will work closely with cross-functional teams to design, test, and deploy autonomous systems that will revolutionize our industry.</p> <p><strong>Key Responsibilities:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Lead the development and implementation of autonomous systems, including software, hardware, and sensors.</li> <li>Collaborate with cross-functional teams to identify business needs and translate them into technical requirements for autonomous systems.</li> <li>Design and develop algorithms and models for autonomous systems, including perception, planning, and control.</li> <li>Test and validate autonomous systems, ensuring they meet safety and performance standards.</li> <li>Continuously improve and optimize autonomous systems based on real-world data and feedback.</li> <li>Stay up-to-date with the latest advancements in autonomous systems technology, and identify opportunities for their integration into our products.</li> <li>Provide technical guidance and leadership to junior engineers, and mentor them in their professional growth.</li> <li>Collaborate with external partners and vendors to source components and technologies for autonomous systems.</li> <li>Participate in industry conferences and events to showcase our company's autonomous systems capabilities.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Qualifications:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Bachelor's degree in Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, Robotics, or a related field. Master's or Ph.D. preferred.</li> <li>Minimum of 8 years of experience in the development of autonomous systems, with at least 3 years in a leadership role.</li> <li>Strong background in software development, including proficiency in programming languages such as Python, C++, and Java.</li> <li>Experience with simulation tools and environments for autonomous systems, such as ROS, Gazebo, or CARLA.</li> <li>Deep understanding of machine learning and deep learning techniques, and their application to autonomous systems.</li> <li>Proven track record in successfully delivering complex projects involving autonomous systems.</li> <li>Excellent problem-solving and analytical skills, with a detail-oriented and systematic approach to work.</li> <li>Strong communication and collaboration skills, with the ability to work effectively in a team environment.</li> <li>Passion for emerging technologies and their potential to drive innovation and growth.</li> </ul> <p>If you have a passion for autonomous systems and are looking for a challenging and rewarding career, we would love to hear from you. Apply now and join our team of talented engineers in shaping the future of autonomous systems.</p><p></p></div></span></div><div class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container"><div <p><strong>Salary:</strong> $123 Per hour</p> <p>Lobox is seeking a highly skilled and experienced Senior Autonomous Systems Engineer to join our dynamic team. As a Senior Autonomous Systems Engineer, you will be responsible for the design, development, and implementation of advanced autonomous systems and technologies.</p> <p><strong>Key Responsibilities:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Lead the design and development of autonomous systems, including autonomous vehicles, drones, and robotics</li> <li>Develop and implement algorithms for perception, planning, and control of autonomous systems</li> <li>Collaborate with cross-functional teams to integrate sensors, hardware, and software components</li> <li>Conduct thorough testing and validation of autonomous systems to ensure functionality and safety</li> <li>Monitor and analyze data from autonomous systems to identify areas for improvement and optimization</li> <li>Stay up-to-date with the latest advancements and trends in autonomous systems and incorporate them into the development process</li> <li>Mentor and provide guidance to junior engineers on autonomous systems development</li> </ul> <p><strong>Qualifications:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Bachelor's or Master's degree in Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, or a related field</li> <li>Minimum of 5 years of experience in the design and development of autonomous systems</li> <li>Strong proficiency in C++, Python, and ROS (Robot Operating System)</li> <li>Experience with perception, planning, and control algorithms for autonomous systems</li> <li>Experience with integration of sensors, hardware, and software components</li> <li>Excellent problem-solving and analytical skills</li> <li>Strong communication and collaboration skills</li> <li>Ability to work in a fast-paced and dynamic environment</li> </ul> <p>At Lobox, we value creativity, innovation, and teamwork. Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__dirRow shrink-0 items-center gap-4"><span class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container"><svg width="16" height="16" style="display:inline-block;vertical-align:middle;--icon-color:#5384EE" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><use href="/assets/icons/icon-sprite.svg?v=2b58b27b0f#icon-trend"></use></svg></span><span style="font-size:15px;line-height:18px;--typography-color:var(--brand)">Trending</span></div></div><div style="height: 114px;" class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container w-full shrink-0 gap-12"><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__lineNumber index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-bold w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp:2;line-clamp:2;font-size:20px;line-height:28px;--typography-color:var(--smoke_coal)">What Does an Accountant Do? Duties, Types and a Typical Day</span><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__lineNumber index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-regular w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp: 2; font-size: 15px; line-height: 23px; --typography-color: var(--primaryText);">An accountant records, checks and explains an organization's money. In practice, that means recording transactions, reconciling accounts, closing the books each month, preparing financial statements and tax returns, and telling managers what the numbers mean for their decisions. So what does an accountant do on an ordinary Tuesday? It depends on the type of accountant, the employer and the time of year. This guide covers the daily work, the main types, how duties change as you move up, and a simple way to tell whether the job would suit you. What does an accountant do day to day? Most accountants spend their days in spreadsheets and accounting software, matching records against bank statements and invoices, fixing differences, posting journal entries and preparing reports. They also answer questions from managers, clients or auditors. The exact mix depends on whether they work in tax, audit, corporate finance or a small firm. If you are reading accountant job details in a listing, these core duties will appear in almost every one: Recording transactions. Entering sales, purchases, payroll and expenses in the general ledger, or reviewing entries that software has posted automatically. Reconciling accounts. Checking that the ledger matches bank statements, credit card statements and supplier records, then finding out why it does not. Month-end and year-end close. Making adjustments, accruals and corrections so the books are complete for the period. Preparing financial statements. Balance sheet, income statement and cash flow statement. Tax work. Preparing returns, estimating tax due and keeping records ready for tax authorities. Budgets and forecasts. Comparing actual spending to the plan and explaining the gaps. Supporting audits. Pulling documents and answering auditors' questions. Advising. Telling a manager or business owner what the numbers mean before they hire, buy or cut costs. Accountant vs bookkeeper vs auditor These three roles overlap, which is why people mix them up. The simplest way to separate them is by what each one is responsible for. In small businesses, one person often does both the bookkeeping and the accounting. In larger companies, the roles are split. Types of accountants and what they do Accounting is several jobs under one title. Here are the main paths you will see in job listings. If you are still deciding, public accounting and corporate (management) accounting are the two most common starting points. What accountants do at each career level Your duties change a lot as you gain experience. Early on you do the detailed work. Later you review other people's work and spend more time explaining numbers to leadership. What does a staff accountant do? A staff accountant handles the detailed, recurring work that keeps the books accurate. That includes posting journal entries, reconciling bank and balance sheet accounts, processing or reviewing invoices, and completing assigned month-end tasks. It is the most common entry-level accounting job and where most people learn how a company's books really work. Senior accountant job duties A senior accountant does fewer routine entries and more checking. Typical duties include reviewing staff reconciliations, preparing financial statements, handling complex transactions such as accruals and fixed assets, preparing audit schedules and training newer team members. Many seniors also improve processes, such as cutting days off the month-end close. A sample week for a staff accountant This is an illustration of how a week near month-end often looks in a corporate accounting team. Your week will vary by employer. In mid-month weeks, the pace is usually calmer. That is when accountants work on projects, clean up old balances or help with budgets. What is busy season really like? Workload in accounting comes in waves. In public accounting, the busiest period is usually the run-up to the main tax filing deadline and year-end audits, when longer hours are common. In corporate roles, the pressure is shorter and more regular: a few intense days at every month-end close, and a heavier stretch at year-end. If you want steady, predictable hours, ask about busy season and month-end expectations in every interview. Answers vary a lot between employers. Where do accountants work? Accountants work almost everywhere money moves. The most common employers are: Public accounting firms, from small local practices to large international firms Companies in every industry, in their finance or accounting department Government agencies at federal, state and local level Nonprofits, schools and hospitals Self-employment, serving small businesses and individuals Many roles are now hybrid or remote, especially after the first year or two. Entry-level roles are more often in the office, because that is where you learn fastest. Skills and tools accountants use The job needs more than being good with numbers. The skills employers ask for most often fall into two groups. Hard skills Spreadsheets: lookups, pivot tables, formulas and tidy formatting Accounting software, such as QuickBooks or Xero in small businesses and larger ERP systems such as NetSuite, SAP or Oracle in bigger companies Understanding of accounting principles (GAAP in the US) Reconciliation and attention to detail Soft skills Explaining numbers in plain language to people who are not accountants Chasing information from other teams politely and persistently Managing deadlines when several closes or clients overlap Honesty and judgment, because you often see sensitive information If you are building a resume for accounting roles, our guide to the best skills to put on a resume shows how to list these so recruiters notice them. Do you need a CPA to be an accountant? No. Many accountants work without a CPA license, especially in corporate roles. A bachelor's degree in accounting or a related field is the usual entry requirement. A CPA becomes important if you want to sign audit opinions, move up in public accounting or reach senior finance roles. Requirements are set by each state. Most states require a set amount of college credit, passing the CPA exam and relevant work experience before you can be licensed. Other certifications, such as the CMA for management accountants, can also help depending on the path you choose. How much do accountants earn? Pay depends on location, industry, level and certifications. For current US figures, check the Accountants and Auditors page in the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, which lists median pay and the job outlook. For pay in your city, compare recent job listings in your area. Is accounting the right career for you? Accounting tends to suit people who enjoy order, finishing tasks completely and finding out why two numbers do not match. It is a weaker fit if you dislike routine or deadlines. A quick self-test helps. Answer honestly: Do you get satisfaction from making something add up exactly? Can you handle a few weeks a year of long hours if the rest of the year is steadier? Are you comfortable asking colleagues for missing documents, more than once? Would you enjoy explaining numbers to people who find them confusing? Are you willing to keep learning as tax rules and software change? If you said yes to most, accounting is worth a closer look. The best next step is to speak with people already doing the job. Two or three short conversations with working accountants will tell you more about busy season, culture and career paths than any article. You can find and connect with finance and accounting professionals on Lobox and ask them what their week actually looks like. How to get started in accounting Pick a starting path. Public accounting if you want fast learning and a clear route to a CPA. Corporate accounting if you want steadier hours. Get the basics. A degree in accounting is the standard route. Career changers often start with accounting coursework or an entry-level role such as accounts payable or bookkeeping. Build practical skills. Get comfortable with spreadsheets and at least one accounting software package. Write a targeted resume. Coming from another field? Our career change resume guide shows how to present your past experience for a new role. Search in the right places. Use specialist and general job search websites, and build connections with accountants and finance recruiters. Prepare for interviews. Expect questions on reconciliations, attention to detail and how you handle deadlines. Our job interview tips cover the basics. Accounting is one of many careers we explain in plain terms. If you are weighing it against tech, see what a software engineer does day to day. Ready to take the next step? If accounting sounds like a fit, start building your network now. Join Lobox to connect with accountants, finance professionals and recruiters, and keep an eye on accounting roles that match your level. Already work in accounting? Share what your typical week looks like in the comments. Real answers help people decide. FAQ 1.What does an accountant do for a small business? For a small business, an accountant usually keeps the books accurate, prepares tax returns, files on time and explains how the business is doing. Many also help with budgets, payroll questions and decisions such as whether you can afford to hire. Some owners use an accountant monthly, others only at tax time. 2. Is being an accountant stressful? It can be, mostly around deadlines. Month-end close, year-end and tax season bring pressure and sometimes long hours. Outside those periods, many accountants describe the work as steady and predictable. Stress levels vary a lot by employer, so ask about busy season and team size before you accept an offer. 3. What is the difference between an accountant and a CPA? An accountant is anyone working in accounting. A CPA is an accountant who has met their state's education and experience rules and passed the CPA exam. Only licensed CPAs can sign audit opinions, and the license often helps with promotion in public accounting and senior finance roles. 4. Do accountants only work with taxes? No. Tax is one specialty. Many accountants never prepare a tax return. They work on monthly closes, financial statements, budgets, cost analysis, audits or fraud investigations. If tax work does not appeal to you, management accounting, internal audit or corporate accounting are common alternatives. 5. Can I become an accountant without an accounting degree? Yes, though the path is longer. Career changers often start in accounts payable, bookkeeping or an accounting assistant role, take accounting courses, and move up with experience. A CPA license has formal education requirements, so check your state board's rules if that is your long-term goal. 6. What does a staff accountant do in their first year? In the first year, a staff accountant mostly learns the company's close process. Expect reconciliations, journal entries, invoice reviews and supporting the senior accountant. You will make corrections, learn the software and gradually take ownership of a set of accounts each month.</span></div></div><div class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp:2;line-clamp:2;font-size:20px;line-height:28px;--typography-color:var(--smoke_coal)">Applicant Tracking System Resume: Rules + Free Template</span><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__lineNumber index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-regular w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp: 2; font-size: 15px; line-height: 23px; --typography-color: var(--primaryText);">Applicant Tracking System Resume: Format Rules and a Free ATS-Friendly Template An applicant tracking system resume is a resume formatted so hiring software can read it correctly: one column, standard section headings, plain fonts, contact details in the main body, and keywords taken from the job post. Get those right and your resume lands in the recruiter's queue looking the way you wrote it. Below you'll find a free ATS-friendly resume template in Word, the formatting rules that matter, a filled example, and a two-minute test you can run on your current resume before you hit apply. What is an applicant tracking system resume? An applicant tracking system (ATS) is the software employers use to collect applications, store candidate profiles and move people through hiring stages. An applicant tracking system resume is simply one the software can parse into the right fields (name, job titles, dates, skills) without scrambling the text, so a recruiter can find and read it. The parsing part is the important bit. When you upload a file, the ATS pulls the text out and sorts it into a candidate record. If your layout confuses it, your job title might end up in the wrong field or your contact details might go missing. The recruiter then sees a messy profile, or doesn't find you in a keyword search at all. Do applicant tracking systems reject resumes automatically? Mostly no. In an Enhancv study of 25 US recruiters (September to October 2025), 23 said their ATS does not auto-reject resumes. A person still makes the call. The automatic rejections that do happen usually come from knockout questions, such as work authorization, a required license or location. You've probably seen the claim that 75% of resumes are rejected by software before a human looks at them. It gets repeated everywhere, usually with no study behind it. The recruiters in that study pointed to something more ordinary: volume. A popular role can attract far more applicants than anyone can read closely, so recruiters search and filter. That changes what you should focus on: • Readability. If the ATS parses your resume badly, a recruiter skimming the profile sees a mess. • Searchability. Recruiters search candidate databases by job title and skill. If your resume never uses the words they search for, you don't show up. • Knockout questions. Answer them honestly and carefully. A wrong click on "Are you authorized to work in the US?" does more damage than any font choice. Some ATS platforms also show AI match or fit scores. In the same study, 11 of the 25 recruiters had them, and most used the score as a guide rather than a decision. Free ATS-friendly resume template (Word) [Download the free ATS-friendly resume template (.docx)] This template is built for parsing first and looks clean enough for the human who reads it next. It's a Word file, so it opens in Microsoft Word, Google Docs and LibreOffice. What's inside: • One column, no tables, text boxes, icons or graphics • Contact details in the body of the page, not in the header • Standard headings: Summary, Skills, Work Experience, Education, Certifications • Word's built-in bullet points and heading styles • Calibri 11 pt body text with simple bold for job titles • Dates written the same way throughout ("Mar 2024 - Present") Here's the structure, so you can see it before you download: [FIRST NAME LAST NAME] [Target Job Title, copied from the job post] [City, State] | [Phone] | [email@example.com] | [Profile URL] SUMMARY [Job title] with [X] years of experience in [2 to 3 core areas from the job post]. Known for [one specific strength backed by a result]. SKILLS [Hard skill 1], [Hard skill 2], [Software or tool], [Certification or method] WORK EXPERIENCE [Job Title] [Company Name] | [City, State or Remote] | [Mon YYYY] - Present • [Action verb] + [what you did] + [result with a number, if you have one] • [Action verb] + [a responsibility that matches a keyword in the job post] EDUCATION [Degree, Major] [School Name] | [City, State] | [YYYY] CERTIFICATIONS [Certification Name], [Issuing Organization], [YYYY] Replace every bracket, delete sections you don't need, and keep it to one or two pages. ATS resume formatting rules that matter The applicant tracking system resume format comes down to one idea: make it easy for software to pull your text out in the right order. Here's what to do and what to avoid. Layout: keep it to one column Some well-built two-column templates parse fine. The trouble is you can't know which system each employer uses, so a single column is the safe default. It also reads well on a phone, which is where plenty of recruiters skim. Section headings: use the boring names Creative headings look nice and parse badly. "Work Experience" or "Professional Experience" tells the software exactly what follows. Save the personality for your summary and bullet points. Contact details: put them in the body Type your name, phone, email, city and profile link as normal text at the top of the page. Don't tuck them into Word's header area. Leave out your full street address; city and state are enough. File name: make it easy to find Name the file "Firstname-Lastname-Resume.docx" or add the job title. "resume_final_v3.docx" doesn't help anyone. Which sections should an ATS-friendly resume include? Use this order for most roles: 1. Contact details. Name, target job title, city and state, phone, email, profile link. 2. Summary. Two or three lines on who you are and what you bring. Our resume summary examples show how to write one fast. 3. Skills. Hard skills, tools and certifications that match the job post. See our list of skills to put on a resume if you're stuck. 4. Work experience. Reverse chronological order, newest first. 5. Education. Degree, school, year (the year is optional if it was a long time ago). 6. Certifications, projects or volunteer work. Only if they support the role. If you're early in your career, an objective statement can replace the summary. If you're switching fields, our career change resume guide covers how to lead with transferable skills while keeping the same ATS-safe layout. How to add keywords from the job post Keywords are the job titles, skills, tools and certifications a recruiter is likely to search for. You find them in the job post itself. 1. Copy the job post into a document. Highlight hard skills, tools, certifications and the exact job title. 2. Mark the repeats. Words that show up in the title, the requirements and the responsibilities are the ones that matter most. 3. Match the employer's wording where it's true. If they say "customer success" and you wrote "client support", use their phrase if it honestly describes your work. 4. Put keywords where they make sense. Your title line, summary, skills section and bullet points. A skill shown in a real bullet carries more weight with the human reader than a skill only listed. 5. Include both forms of acronyms once. "Search engine optimization (SEO)" covers both ways someone might search. 6. Leave out what you can't back up. If a recruiter asks about it in the interview, you need a real example. Don't paste the job description in white text or repeat a keyword ten times. Recruiters see the parsed text, and stuffing makes you look worse, not better. Applying to several similar roles? Keep a master resume and tailor a copy for each application. Browsing a batch of open roles on Lobox is a quick way to spot the skills and job titles that keep coming up in your field, so you know which keywords belong in your master version. Applicant tracking system resume example Here's a filled example for a customer success role. Every detail is fictional; copy the structure, not the content. JORDAN REYES Customer Success Manager Austin, TX | (555) 010-2468 | jordan.reyes@email.com | [profile URL] SUMMARY Customer success manager with 5 years of experience in B2B SaaS onboarding, account renewals and customer training. Known for turning at-risk accounts into renewals through structured check-ins and clear success plans. SKILLS Customer onboarding, Account management, Renewals and upsells, Salesforce, Zendesk, Gainsight, QBR planning, Customer training, Churn analysis WORK EXPERIENCE Customer Success Manager Brightline Software | Austin, TX | Mar 2022 - Present • Manage a portfolio of 60 mid-market accounts, leading onboarding, quarterly business reviews and renewal planning • Built a 30-day onboarding checklist used by the whole CS team • Partner with sales on upsell opportunities identified during QBRs Customer Support Specialist Northfield Apps | Remote | Jun 2019 - Feb 2022 • Resolved technical and billing tickets in Zendesk across email and chat • Wrote 40+ help center articles on common setup questions EDUCATION B.A., Communication University of Texas at Austin | Austin, TX | 2019 Notice what it does: the exact job title sits under the name, the skills line mirrors a typical customer success job post, and the keywords show up again inside real bullet points. How to test your resume before you apply You don't need a paid tool to run a basic applicant tracking system resume test. Try this: 1. Copy and paste test. Open your file, select all, copy, and paste into a plain text editor (Notepad, TextEdit in plain text mode). Read it top to bottom. 2. Check the order. Your name should come first, then contact details, then sections in order. If lines from two columns are mixed together, that's what a parser may see. 3. Check for missing text. If your email, phone or job titles are gone, they were probably in a header, text box or graphic. 4. Check for strange characters. Boxes, question marks or broken symbols mean a font or bullet didn't convert. 5. PDF users: try selecting the text. If you can't highlight words in your PDF, it's an image and an ATS can't read it. Free and paid applicant tracking system resume check tools can add a keyword comparison against a job post. Treat the score as a hint, not a pass or fail. No checker knows how a specific employer has set up its system. Pre-submit checklist • One column, no tables, text boxes, icons or photos • Name and contact details in the body, not the header • Standard section headings • Exact job title from the post near the top • Keywords from the job post in the summary, skills and bullets • Same date format everywhere • File type matches what the job post asks for • File named with your name • Plain text paste test done • Knockout questions answered carefully Ready to apply? A clean ATS-friendly resume gets you read. Tailoring it to each role gets you a call back. Download the template, run the paste test, then put it to work: browse open roles and apply to jobs on Lobox, where you can also connect with recruiters hiring in your field. Apply to jobs on Lobox FAQ Is a PDF or Word resume better for an ATS? Follow the job post first. If it asks for a specific file type, use it. If it doesn't say, a .docx file is the safest choice because nearly every system reads it. A text-based PDF exported from Word or Google Docs is usually fine too. Avoid scanned PDFs and image files, since there's no text inside for the software to read. Are Canva resume templates ATS-friendly? Some are, many aren't. Canva designs often rely on columns, text boxes, icons and graphics, which can scramble or hide text when an ATS extracts it. If you love a Canva design, export it, then paste the text into a plain text editor. If the order is jumbled or details are missing, switch to a single-column Word template for online applications. Can an ATS read a two-column resume? Sometimes. Some systems handle clean two-column layouts, while others read straight across the page and mix lines from both columns. Since you can't tell which system an employer uses, a single column is the lower-risk option. If you keep two columns, run the copy and paste test and check that each section comes out whole and in order. How long should an applicant tracking system resume be? One page works for most early-career candidates. Two pages is normal once you have several relevant roles or a long list of projects. The ATS itself doesn't penalize a second page. Length matters to the recruiter reading it, so cut anything that doesn't support the job you're applying for. Do I need to tailor my resume for every application? You don't need to rewrite it, but you should adjust it. Update the job title line, reorder your skills to match the post, and swap in the employer's wording where it honestly fits your experience. Keep a master resume with everything, then save a tailored copy for each role so you can track what you sent where. Are Google Docs resume templates ATS-friendly? The simple, single-column Google Docs templates usually are. Watch out for templates that use tables or side panels to create their layout, since those can break up the text. Download your finished resume as .docx or PDF, then run the plain text paste test before you upload it anywhere.</span></div></div><div class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp:2;line-clamp:2;font-size:20px;line-height:28px;--typography-color:var(--smoke_coal)">How to Write a Cover Letter (Step-by-Step Guide with Template)</span><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__lineNumber index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-regular w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp: 2; font-size: 15px; line-height: 23px; --typography-color: var(--primaryText);">To write a cover letter, pick the three things the job post asks for most, then show in under a page how you've already done them. Open with the role and your strongest match, back it up with one or two specific examples, and close by asking for a conversation. That's the whole method. Below you'll find how to write a cover letter for a job step by step, a template you can copy, two examples, and a checklist to run before you hit send. What is a cover letter for a job? A cover letter is a short letter, usually one page, that you send with your resume when you apply for a job. Your resume lists what you've done. The cover letter explains why that experience fits this specific role and this specific company, in your own voice. It's your chance to connect the dots for the hiring manager. Not every employer reads them, and some applications make them optional. Write one anyway when the job matters to you. A tailored letter is one of the few parts of an application where you control the story. How to write a cover letter in 6 steps Step 1: Pull three requirements from the job post Before you write a word, open the job description and highlight what comes up most. Look at the first few bullet points, anything repeated, and anything marked "required". Pick the top three. For each, note one moment from your work where you did that thing and what happened as a result. Those three pairs are the raw material for your whole letter. Step 2: Write the header Keep it simple and match the look of your resume. Include: • Your full name • Phone number and professional email • City and state (a full street address is optional) • A link to your portfolio or professional profile, if relevant • The date • The hiring manager's name, title and company If you're pasting the letter into an online form or an email, skip the date and the employer's address block. Put your contact details under your signature instead. Step 3: Address it to a real person The best way to address a cover letter is by name: "Dear Priya Sharma" or "Dear Ms. Sharma". If you don't know their title or pronouns, the full name is the safe choice. To find the name, check the job post, the company's team page, or professional networks. If you still can't find it, use a specific team greeting: • Dear Hiring Manager • Dear Marketing Team • Dear [Company Name] Recruiting Team Avoid "To whom it may concern". It reads like a form letter, which is the opposite of what you want. Step 4: Open with the job and your strongest match Your first two sentences decide whether the rest gets read. Name the role, then lead with the single best reason you fit. Skip "My name is" and "I am writing to apply". They already know. Weak: "I am writing to express my interest in the Account Manager position at your company." Better: "I'm applying for the Account Manager role at Brightline because I've spent three years doing exactly what your post describes: keeping a large book of B2B clients happy and renewing." If someone referred you, mention them here. It's the strongest opener you can have. Step 5: Prove it in one or two body paragraphs This is where your three pairs from Step 1 go. Write one short paragraph per point, or group them into two paragraphs if they're related. Use this simple pattern for each one: 1. The need: what the company wants 2. The proof: what you did, with a number or clear result if you have one 3. The link: how that helps them in this role Don't repeat your resume line by line. Pick the stories behind the bullet points. Add one sentence about why this company specifically, based on something real: a product you use, a recent launch, or how they describe their team. Step 6: End with a clear next step To end a cover letter well, sum up your fit in one line, thank them, and invite a conversation. Then sign off. "I'd welcome the chance to talk about how I could help your team keep renewals on track. Thank you for your time, and I look forward to hearing from you." Good sign-offs: "Best regards", "Kind regards", "Sincerely". Then your full name. Avoid casual closers like "Cheers" unless the company's tone is clearly informal. Cover letter template (copy and paste) Copy this into your document, then replace every bracket. Delete any line that doesn't apply. [Your Name] [Phone] | [Email] | [City, State] | [Portfolio or profile link] [Date] [Hiring Manager Name] [Title] [Company] Dear [Hiring Manager Name], I'm applying for the [Job Title] role at [Company] because [one-line reason you fit, tied to the top requirement in the job post]. In my role as [your current or last title] at [company], I [specific achievement linked to requirement 1, with a result]. I also [achievement linked to requirement 2], which [result or benefit]. What draws me to [Company] is [something specific: product, mission, recent news, team culture]. I'd bring [requirement 3 skill], shown by [short proof], to help your team [goal from the job post]. I'd welcome the chance to talk about how I can help with [main priority of the role]. Thank you for your time and consideration. Best regards, [Your Name] Cover letter examples Both examples are fictional and written for this guide. Use them to check your structure and tone, not to copy word for word. Example 1: Entry-level (customer support role) Dear Jordan Lee, I'm applying for the Customer Support Associate role at Nestwell. I spent two years answering customer questions part-time while finishing my degree, and I enjoy turning a frustrated caller into a satisfied one. At the campus bookstore, I handled phone and email queries during the busiest weeks of each semester. I wrote a short FAQ for common order problems, which my manager shared with the whole team. Your post mentions documenting solutions for the knowledge base, and that's the part of the job I'm most excited about. I've used Nestwell's app to manage my own rental, so I know the product from the customer's side. I'd love to bring that view to your support team. Thank you for considering my application. I'd be glad to talk whenever suits you. Kind regards, Sam Ortiz Example 2: Experienced (operations coordinator) Dear Hiring Manager, I'm applying for the Operations Coordinator position at Fieldstone Logistics. For the past five years, I've run scheduling and vendor coordination for a regional distribution team, which lines up closely with what your post describes. In my current role, I moved our delivery scheduling from spreadsheets to a shared planning tool and trained eight dispatchers to use it. Missed delivery windows dropped noticeably in the first quarter. I also manage relationships with 20+ vendors, including contract renewals and performance reviews. Fieldstone's expansion into two new states will need tight coordination between warehouses and carriers. That's the work I do every day, and I'd like to do it for a team that's growing. I'd welcome a conversation about how I could support your operations team. Thank you for your time. Best regards, Dana Mitchell How long should a cover letter be? A cover letter should fit on one page, which usually means three to four short paragraphs and roughly 250 to 400 words. If you're pasting it into an email or an application form, aim for the shorter end. Hiring managers skim, so every sentence should earn its place. If yours runs long, cut in this order: anything that repeats your resume, general claims without proof ("I'm a hard worker"), and any second example for the same skill. Cover letter vs resume: what's the difference? A resume is a structured record of your experience, skills and education. A cover letter is a short, personal argument for why that experience fits one specific job. You can reuse a resume across similar roles, but every cover letter should be written for the job in front of you. Want your resume to match the letter? Our guides on the best skills to put on a resume and resume summary examples help you line up both documents. How to tailor your cover letter in 5 minutes You don't need to start from scratch for every application. Keep a master version built from the template above, then change these four things each time: 1. The greeting. Find a real name if you can. 2. The opening line. Swap in the job title and the top requirement from this post. 3. One body example. Pick the story that best matches this role's main need. 4. The "why this company" sentence. Make it specific to them. Finding a real name is often the hardest part. On Lobox you can connect with professionals and recruiters, which makes it easier to find out who's hiring for a team before you apply. Should you use AI to write your cover letter? AI tools can help you get a first draft down or tighten a paragraph that runs long. The risk is a letter that sounds like everyone else's: generic praise for the company, vague claims and no real examples. If you use AI, feed it your three requirement-and-proof pairs from Step 1 and the job post. Then rewrite the result in your own words, check every fact, and remove anything you couldn't back up in an interview. Common cover letter mistakes to avoid • Sending the same letter to every employer • Opening with "My name is" or "I am writing to apply" • Repeating your resume instead of telling the story behind it • Talking only about what you want, not what you'll bring • Getting the company name or job title wrong (it happens more than you'd think) • Going over one page Checklist before you send • Addressed to a named person, or a specific team • Job title and company name are correct • Opening line names the role and your strongest match • At least one example with a clear result • One sentence on why this company • Under one page • Read out loud once for typos and awkward phrasing • Saved as PDF unless the employer asked for another format, with a clear file name (FirstName-LastName-Cover-Letter.pdf) Once your letter is ready, the interview is the next step. Our job interview tips cover how to prepare. Ready to put your cover letter to work? A good cover letter only helps if it reaches the right job. Join Lobox to find jobs that match your experience, connect with recruiters, and apply with a letter that's written for the role. FAQ Do I really need a cover letter? If the application asks for one, yes. If it's optional, send one for any job you genuinely want, because it lets you explain your fit in a way a resume can't. Skip it only when the application system has no place to add one, or the employer says not to. What should a cover letter include? Your contact details, a greeting addressed to a person or team, an opening that names the role and your strongest match, one or two paragraphs of proof tied to the job post, a line on why this company, and a closing that invites a conversation. Keep it all on one page. How do you start a cover letter? Start with the job title and the single best reason you fit, in one or two sentences. If someone referred you, name them first. Avoid stock openers like "My name is" or "I am writing to apply", because the reader already knows who you are and why the letter exists. Is it OK to write "Dear Hiring Manager"? Yes, when you can't find a name. It's polite and widely accepted. A named greeting is better, so spend a few minutes checking the job post, the company website and professional networks first. A specific team greeting, like "Dear Marketing Team", is a good middle ground. Should my cover letter be a PDF or Word file? Use PDF unless the employer asks for something else. A PDF keeps your formatting the same on every screen. If the application asks for a Word document, or you're pasting into a text box, follow those instructions instead. Name the file clearly with your name and "Cover Letter". Can I use the same cover letter for every job? You can reuse the structure, but not the letter itself. Keep a master version, then change the greeting, opening line, main example and the "why this company" sentence for each application. A generic letter is easy to spot and usually does more harm than sending none.</span></div></div><div class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__truncate index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-regular min-w-0" style="font-size:14px;line-height:18px;--typography-color:var(--secondaryDisabledText)">Information Technology &amp; Services</span></div><div class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__dirRow shrink-0 items-center gap-4"><span class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container"><svg width="16" height="16" style="display:inline-block;vertical-align:middle;--icon-color:#5384EE" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><use href="/assets/icons/icon-sprite.svg?v=2b58b27b0f#icon-trend"></use></svg></span><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-medium" style="font-size:15px;line-height:18px;--typography-color:var(--brand)">Trending</span></div></div><div style="height: 114px;" class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container w-full shrink-0 gap-12"><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__lineNumber index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-bold w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp:2;line-clamp:2;font-size:20px;line-height:28px;--typography-color:var(--smoke_coal)">Customer Service Training: 12 Essential Topics Every Team Should Cover</span><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__lineNumber index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-regular w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp: 2; font-size: 15px; line-height: 23px; --typography-color: var(--primaryText);">Customer service is more than answering questions and resolving complaints. It is about creating positive experiences, building customer trust, and developing long-term relationships. For businesses operating in competitive markets, the quality of customer support can directly influence customer satisfaction, brand reputation, and business growth. However, excellent customer service does not happen automatically. Employees need proper training, practical experience, and a clear understanding of customer expectations. Without the right skills, even experienced employees may struggle to handle difficult conversations, resolve complaints, or provide consistent support. Customer service training helps employees communicate effectively, understand customer needs, solve problems, and represent a company professionally. Whether a business operates through physical stores, websites, mobile applications, or social media, investing in employee development is essential. Let's explore 12 important customer service training topics every organization should include in its training program. 1. Effective Communication Skills Communication is the foundation of excellent customer service. Employees interact with customers through phone calls, emails, live chats, and face-to-face conversations. Each interaction requires clarity, professionalism, and appropriate language. Training should focus on clear verbal and written communication, professional email and chat responses, appropriate tone and language, asking relevant questions, and explaining complicated information simply. Practical example: When a customer complains about a delayed delivery, an employee should acknowledge the concern, explain the reason for the delay, and communicate the expected delivery date. Good communication reduces misunderstandings and creates a more positive customer experience. 2. Understanding Customer Needs and Expectations Every customer has different expectations. Some want quick answers, while others need detailed explanations before making a decision. Customer service representatives should learn how to identify customer requirements instead of immediately offering generic solutions. Training should include understanding customer behavior, asking relevant questions, identifying problems, and confirming customer expectations. For example, if a customer contacts a software company because an application is not working, the representative should first understand the problem, device, and circumstances before suggesting a solution. Understanding customer needs helps employees provide relevant and personalized assistance. 3. Active Listening and Empathy Active listening means giving customers full attention and understanding their concerns without interrupting them. Empathy means recognizing how customers feel and responding with understanding and respect. Employees should learn to listen without interrupting, avoid assumptions, acknowledge customer concerns, ask questions for clarification, and respond calmly. Example: Saying “I understand how frustrating this situation must be. Let me help you resolve it” can make a difficult interaction more positive. Empathy helps build trust and makes customers feel valued. 4. Problem-Solving and Complaint Handling Resolving customer problems is one of the most important responsibilities of a customer service team. Employees must know how to identify issues, investigate their causes, explain possible solutions, and follow up when necessary. Common situations covered during training include delayed deliveries, incorrect billing information, refund and cancellation requests, product defects, technical difficulties, and poor service experiences. Companies should conduct role-playing exercises where employees practice responding to realistic customer complaints. A structured problem-solving approach helps teams resolve issues efficiently while maintaining professionalism. 5. Product and Service Knowledge Employees cannot provide accurate assistance without understanding the products or services they represent. Product knowledge training should cover features, benefits, pricing, usage instructions, company policies, limitations, and frequently asked questions. Businesses should regularly update training materials whenever products, services, or policies change. For example, a customer support employee working for an e-commerce company should understand order tracking, payment methods, return policies, and refund procedures. Strong product knowledge increases employee confidence and helps customers receive accurate information. 6. Time Management and Response Handling Customers expect timely responses, especially when dealing with urgent problems. Customer service teams must learn how to manage multiple requests without compromising service quality. Important training areas include prioritizing urgent customer issues, managing multiple conversations, following response-time guidelines, organizing support tickets, completing customer follow-ups, and maintaining accuracy while working efficiently. Employees should understand that faster responses are valuable, but providing incorrect information just to save time can create additional problems. 7. Customer Relationship Management (CRM) Tools Customer Relationship Management (CRM) software helps businesses organize customer information, track interactions, manage support requests, and maintain communication history. Customer service employees should receive practical training on the CRM systems used by their organization. Important CRM skills include creating and updating customer records, managing support tickets, tracking previous interactions, assigning requests to relevant departments, scheduling follow-ups, and generating customer service reports. CRM knowledge helps employees provide consistent support and reduces the need for customers to repeat information. 8. Handling Difficult and Angry Customers Not every customer interaction is easy. Some customers may be frustrated because of delayed services, unexpected charges, technical issues, or unmet expectations. Employees should learn how to remain calm, avoid arguments, and focus on finding practical solutions. Training should cover conflict management, professional language, emotional control, escalation procedures, and complaint resolution. An important principle is to focus on resolving the customer's problem rather than proving who is right. If an issue cannot be resolved at the employee level, it should be escalated to the appropriate supervisor. 9. Data Privacy and Customer Security Customer service representatives often handle personal details, contact information, account records, and transaction-related information. Protecting this information is essential for maintaining customer trust and following organizational security policies. Training should include password protection, customer identity verification, secure communication practices, confidential information handling, access permissions, and recognizing suspicious requests. Employees should never disclose customer information without proper authorization. A strong understanding of data privacy helps reduce security risks and protects both customers and businesses. 10. Multichannel Customer Support Customers expect businesses to provide support through different communication channels. These may include phone calls, emails, live chat, social media, messaging applications, and website contact forms. Each channel requires a slightly different communication approach. Training employees across these channels helps businesses maintain consistent service quality. 11. Teamwork and Cross-Department Collaboration Customer service is not always an individual responsibility. Some customer issues require support from technical teams, sales departments, finance teams, or management. Employees should understand how to share information, transfer requests, coordinate responsibilities, and communicate effectively with other departments. For example, a billing-related complaint may require assistance from the finance department, while a software issue may need technical support. Effective teamwork reduces delays and helps customers receive complete solutions. 12. Measuring Customer Service Performance Customer service training should also explain how businesses evaluate service quality and employee performance. Organizations use different performance indicators to understand whether customers are receiving effective support. Some important customer service metrics include: Employees should understand these metrics and how their daily activities influence customer experience. How to Create an Effective Customer Service Training Program Simply explaining customer service concepts is not enough. Businesses should combine theoretical learning with practical exercises. Role-Playing Activities: Create realistic customer situations and allow employees to practice their responses. Product Demonstrations: Provide hands-on experience with products, services, and company systems. Regular Workshops: Conduct sessions covering communication, problem-solving, and customer relationship management. Performance Feedback: Review customer interactions and provide constructive suggestions for improvement. Continuous Learning: Update training materials whenever customer expectations, company policies, or business processes change. A structured training program helps employees improve their skills gradually and apply what they learn in real customer interactions. The Role of Digital Platforms in Professional Development Professional development does not end after initial employee training. Employees need opportunities to exchange knowledge, learn about industry trends, and develop new professional connections. Digital platforms make it easier for individuals to share ideas, discover useful information, and connect with other professionals. Platforms such as Lobox contribute to the digital networking ecosystem by focusing on professional connections, content sharing, and opportunity discovery. Access to professional communities and useful learning resources can support continuous development across different industries. Conclusion Customer service training is an important investment for businesses that want to improve customer satisfaction and build stronger relationships. From communication and active listening to CRM tools, problem-solving, data privacy, and performance measurement, every training topic contributes to better service quality. Organizations should regularly evaluate their training programs, provide practical learning opportunities, and encourage employees to improve their skills. A well-trained customer service team does more than answer questions. It builds customer trust, resolves problems, protects brand reputation, and contributes to long-term business success. Ultimately, excellent customer service begins with well-trained employees who understand that every customer interaction is an opportunity to create a positive experience.</span></div></div><div shrink-0 gap-12"><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__lineNumber index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-bold w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp:2;line-clamp:2;font-size:20px;line-height:28px;--typography-color:var(--smoke_coal)">Boeing China Order: Xiamen Airlines Buys 50 737 MAX Jets</span><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__lineNumber index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-regular w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp: 2; font-size: 15px; line-height: 23px; --typography-color: var(--primaryText);">SEATTLE, Nov. 25, 2026 Boeing China Order: Xiamen Airlines Buys 50 737 MAX Jets Boeing has landed its biggest order from a Chinese airline since 2017. Xiamen Airlines, a subsidiary of China Southern Airlines, agreed on Tuesday to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 jets at a list price of about $7.4 billion, according to a stock exchange filing by China Southern. The deal is a clear win for Boeing after years of being frozen out of one of the world's largest aviation markets. But the headline number hides a few important details. What is in the Boeing China deal? The order covers 50 single-aisle 737 MAX 8 planes. The $7.4 billion figure is the list price. China Southern said Boeing offered a significant discount, so the real price will be lower. Big discounts are standard on large aircraft orders, and the final amount was not disclosed. The jets will not arrive soon. Deliveries are planned in batches from 2031 to 2034. The deal also still needs approval from China Southern's shareholders and Chinese government authorities. China Southern said the planes will support Xiamen Airlines' move to the new Xiamen Xiang'an airport and help build an aviation hub in Fujian province Boeing declined to comment and referred questions to the airline, KOMO News reported. Why this order matters for Boeing Boeing had gone almost a decade without a major order from a Chinese airline. During the trade war that followed U.S. tariffs, China reportedly told its airlines last year to stop taking Boeing deliveries. The new order follows a commitment China made to buy 200 Boeing jets during a May summit in Beijing between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. The filing does not say whether these 50 planes count toward that pledge. Scott Hamilton, an aviation analyst at Leeham Co., told KOMO News that China has used plane orders as a political signal for years. When Beijing was unhappy with Washington, he said, "Airbus got the orders." He called this deal a sign that relations are good enough for now, but warned it "doesn't mean the floodgates are open." Is China really back as a Boeing customer? Not fully, at least not yet. In April, China Southern and Xiamen Airlines agreed to buy 137 Airbus A320neo-family jets. That is almost three times the size of this Boeing order, from the same airline group. Xiamen Airlines also flew only Boeing planes for nearly four decades before it added its first leased Airbus A321neo in early 2023. So this order brings Boeing back into a relationship it used to own, rather than opening a new market. Political expectations are running ahead of confirmed deals. On Monday, Trump said China would buy another 250 Boeing planes. Chinese officials have not confirmed any further purchases. In September, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said about 140 jetliner orders were in a good state. What it means for Boeing workers and suppliers Long-dated orders like this help Boeing and its suppliers plan production further ahead. But since deliveries start in 2031, the deal does little for near-term work on the 737 line in Renton. KOMO News also reported that Boeing plans to cut about 5% of its commercial airplanes workforce, with notices starting in December. Watch for approval from China Southern shareholders and Beijing, which will make the order firm. The next signal is whether China names more specific airlines and aircraft under the 200-jet commitment, or confirms any part of the larger numbers Trump has mentioned.</span></div></div><div class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container w-full shrink-0 gap-12"><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__lineNumber index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-bold w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp:2;line-clamp:2;font-size:20px;line-height:28px;--typography-color:var(--smoke_coal)">Website Development: How to Build a Website Step by Step (With Examples)</span><span class="index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__base index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__lineNumber index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__color index-module-scss-module__nlcBwa__font-regular w-full" style="-webkit-line-clamp: 2; font-size: 15px; line-height: 23px; --typography-color: var(--primaryText);">A website is often the first place where potential customers learn about a business. A well-developed website helps companies present their services, share information, generate leads, and build trust with visitors. However, creating an effective website requires more than choosing a design and publishing a few pages. It involves planning, development, testing, optimization, and regular maintenance. Below, we'll explore what website development means, the different stages involved, the technologies used, common mistakes, and practical examples to help you understand the complete process. What is website development? Website development is the process of creating, building, and maintaining websites. It includes everything from designing the user interface to developing server-side functionality and managing databases. A website can be a simple informational platform, an online store, a business website, or a complex web application. Most websites involve three important components: Frontend: The visual part of a website that visitors interact with. Backend: The server-side functionality that manages requests and application logic. Database: The system used to store and organize information. How does website development work? Website development follows a structured process. Developers first understand the project requirements, select appropriate technologies, create the design, develop the functionality, and test the final product. For example, an e-commerce website requires product pages, shopping cart functionality, payment integration, and customer account management. The development process connects all these elements to create a functional website experience. How to build a website in 7 steps 1. Define your website’s purpose Before starting development, identify what the website needs to achieve. A business website may focus on generating leads, while an e-commerce website may focus on selling products. Define your target audience, business objectives, required features, and expected results. 2. Plan the website structure Create a basic structure showing how different pages will connect. This is commonly known as a sitemap. A business website might include Home, About Us, Services, Portfolio, Blog, and Contact Us. A clear structure helps visitors find information easily. 3. Choose the right technologies Technology selection depends on the website's complexity, functionality, and future requirements. Common technologies include HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, PHP, Java, and MySQL. 4. Design the user interface The design stage focuses on creating an attractive and easy-to-use website. Developers and designers work on layouts, colors, typography, navigation, and responsive elements. The website should work properly on desktops, tablets, and mobile devices. 5. Develop frontend and backend functionality Frontend developers build visible elements, while backend developers manage application logic, databases, and server communication. Both components work together to deliver a complete website experience. 6. Test the website Testing helps identify technical errors before the website goes live. Developers check page loading, navigation, forms, links, responsiveness, and security. 7. Launch and maintain the website After successful testing, the website is deployed to a hosting server. Regular updates, security checks, backups, and performance improvements help keep it reliable. Types of website development Different websites require different development approaches depending on their purpose and functionality. Popular technologies used in website development Choosing suitable technologies can improve website performance, flexibility, and maintainability. Common website development mistakes and how to fix them 1. Ignoring Mobile Responsiveness: A website that works only on desktops can create a poor experience for mobile visitors. Use responsive layouts and test pages on different screen sizes. 2. Slow Website Loading: Large images, unnecessary scripts, and poor hosting can affect loading speed. Optimize images, reduce unnecessary code, and use suitable hosting infrastructure. 3. Poor Navigation: Visitors may leave if they cannot find important information. Use clear menus, logical page structures, and accessible navigation. 4. Ignoring Website Security: Weak passwords, outdated software, and missing security configurations can expose websites to threats. Use HTTPS, regular updates, secure authentication, and appropriate backups. 5. Not Considering SEO: A website without proper SEO practices may struggle to attract organic traffic. Use descriptive page titles, relevant keywords, proper headings, and search-friendly URLs. Website development checklist Before launching a website, review these essential requirements: Website design is responsive. All pages and links work correctly. Contact forms function properly. Website loading speed is optimized. HTTPS security is enabled. SEO titles and meta descriptions are added. Important pages are accessible on mobile devices. Website backups and maintenance plans are available. How much time does website development take? The development timeline depends on the website's size, functionality, design requirements, and available resources. These are general estimates. Actual timelines depend on project requirements and development complexity. What makes a website successful? A successful website combines good design, useful content, reliable functionality, and a smooth user experience. It should clearly communicate its purpose and help visitors complete their intended actions. Performance, mobile responsiveness, security, and regular maintenance are equally important. Businesses should also monitor website analytics to understand visitor behavior and identify areas for improvement. Conclusion Website development is a structured process that combines design, programming, testing, and maintenance. From simple business websites to complex web applications, every project requires proper planning and suitable technologies. By following the right development practices, businesses can create reliable websites that improve their online presence, support customer engagement, and contribute to long-term growth. FAQ 1. What are the main stages of website development? The main stages include planning, designing, frontend development, backend development, testing, deployment, and maintenance. 2. Which programming languages are used for website development? HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PHP, Python, and Java are commonly used for website development. 3. What is the difference between frontend and backend development? Frontend development focuses on the visual and interactive parts of a website, while backend development manages server-side operations, databases, and application logic. 4. How much does it cost to develop a website? Website development costs depend on design, functionality, hosting, technology, and project complexity. A basic website generally costs less than a customized web application. 5. Is website development important for businesses? Yes. A professional website helps businesses establish an online presence, showcase their services, communicate with customers, and generate potential leads. 6. What is the difference between a website and a web application? A website primarily presents information, while a web application offers interactive functionality that allows users to perform specific tasks, such as managing projects or making transactions.</span></div></div><div class="Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__container Flex-component-module-scss-module__Lkixxa__dirRow w-full items-center gap-20"><div style="display:inline-block;vertical-align:middle;--icon-color:#5384EE" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><use href="/assets/icons/icon-sprite.svg?v=2b58b27b0f#icon-trend"></use></svg></span><span
