Here's what to do and what to avoid.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/section\u003e\u003csection data-article-block=\"columns\"\u003e\u003cdiv data-article-column data-width=\"50%\"\u003e\u003cfigure data-article-block=\"image\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.lobox.com/image/original/e7608a0b45aa4c868dabf0dfa2178bcf.webp\" alt=\"\" /\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-article-column data-width=\"50%\"\u003e\u003ch2\u003eLayout: keep it to one column\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp\u003eSome well-built two-column templates parse fine. The trouble is you can't know which system each employer uses, so a single column is the safe default. It also reads well on a phone, which is where plenty of recruiters skim.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch2\u003eSection headings: use the boring names\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp\u003eCreative headings look nice and parse badly. \"Work Experience\" or \"Professional Experience\" tells the software exactly what follows. Save the personality for your summary and bullet points.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch2\u003eContact details: put them in the body\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp\u003eType your name, phone, email, city and profile link as normal text at the top of the page. Don't tuck them into Word's header area. Leave out your full street address; city and state are enough.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch2\u003eFile name: make it easy to find\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp\u003eName the file \"Firstname-Lastname-Resume.docx\" or add the job title. \"resume_final_v3.docx\" doesn't help anyone.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003c/section\u003e\u003csection data-article-block=\"section\"\u003e\u003ch2\u003eWhich sections should an ATS-friendly resume include?\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp\u003eUse this order for most roles:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1. \u003cstrong\u003eContact details.\u003c/strong\u003e Name, target job title, city and state, phone, email, profile link.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2. \u003cstrong\u003eSummary.\u003c/strong\u003e Two or three lines on who you are and what you bring. Our \u003ca href=\"https://lobox.com/articles/92\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eresume summary examples\u003c/a\u003e show how to write one fast.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3. \u003cstrong\u003eSkills.\u003c/strong\u003e Hard skills, tools and certifications that match the job post. If you're switching fields, our \u003ca href=\"https://lobox.com/articles/80\" target=\"_blank\"\u003ecareer change resume\u003c/a\u003e guide covers how to lead with transferable skills while keeping the same ATS-safe layout.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/section\u003e\u003ch2\u003eHow to add keywords from the job post \u003c/h2\u003e\u003csection data-article-block=\"section\"\u003e\u003cp\u003eKeywords are the job titles, skills, tools and certifications a recruiter is likely to search for. You find them in the job post itself.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1. \u003cstrong\u003eCopy the job post into a document.\u003c/strong\u003e Highlight hard skills, tools, certifications and the exact job title.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2. \u003cstrong\u003eMark the repeats.\u003c/strong\u003e Words that show up in the title, the requirements and the responsibilities are the ones that matter most.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3. \u003cstrong\u003eMatch the employer's wording where it's true.\u003c/strong\u003e If they say \"customer success\" and you wrote \"client support\", use their phrase if it honestly describes your work.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4. \u003cstrong\u003ePut keywords where they make sense.\u003c/strong\u003e Your title line, summary, skills section and bullet points. A skill shown in a real bullet carries more weight with the human reader than a skill only listed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e5. \u003cstrong\u003eInclude both forms of acronyms once.\u003c/strong\u003e \"Search engine optimization (SEO)\" covers both ways someone might search.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6. \u003cstrong\u003eLeave out what you can't back up.\u003c/strong\u003e If a recruiter asks about it in the interview, you need a real example.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDon't paste the job description in white text or repeat a keyword ten times. It can't fix a vague job description or convince a strong candidate to choose you. Those parts of hiring stay with you.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/section\u003e\u003csection data-article-block=\"section\"\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eIt can't judge fit or potential\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAI ranks people by how closely their resume matches the job and how similar they look to past patterns. That works against career changers, people returning to work and anyone self-taught.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTake a former teacher applying for a training coordinator role. Her resume says \"lesson planning\" and \"classroom management\", not \"instructional design\" or \"learning programs\". A keyword match ranks her low. A person reading it sees someone who has designed and delivered training every working day for years.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/section\u003e\u003csection data-article-block=\"section\"\u003e\u003ch2\u003eIt can't guarantee fair outcomes\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp\u003eAI learns from data. If your past hires leaned one way, by age, gender or background, a tool trained on that history can learn the same lean and repeat it at scale. Amazon reportedly dropped an experimental resume-screening tool after finding it marked down resumes linked to women \u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCourts are now looking at the software itself. In \u003cem\u003eMobley v. Workday\u003c/em\u003e, filed in 2023, a job applicant alleged that Workday's screening technology discriminated on the basis of age, race and disability. In June 2026 a federal judge refused Workday's request to dismiss the California state-law claims (\u003ca href=\"https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/technology/workday-ai-lawsuit-wake-up-call-hr\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eSHRM\u003c/a\u003e). The case hasn't been decided, but the message for employers is clear: \"the software made the call\" won't protect you.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/section\u003e\u003csection data-article-block=\"section\"\u003e\u003ch2\u003eIt can't keep you compliant on its own\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe rules depend on where you hire. Two US examples:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• \u003cstrong\u003eNew York City:\u003c/strong\u003e Local Law 144 covers automated employment decision tools. Employers using one need an independent bias audit every year, must publish a summary of the results and must tell candidates who live in the city that a tool is being used (\u003ca href=\"https://www.nyc.gov/assets/dca/downloads/pdf/about/DCWP-AEDT-FAQ.pdf\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eNYC DCWP FAQ\u003c/a\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• \u003cstrong\u003eColorado:\u003c/strong\u003e a new law, SB 26-189, replaced the state's 2024 AI Act. It focuses on notice, disclosure, recordkeeping and human review, and takes effect January 1, 2027 (\u003ca href=\"https://www.proskauer.com/blog/colorados-ai-law-gets-major-rewrite-what-now-for-employers\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eProskauer\u003c/a\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFederal anti-discrimination law applies whether or not a tool is involved. This isn't legal advice. If you hire in several states, check with an employment lawyer before you switch on automated screening.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch2\u003eIt can't fix a bad job description\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf your requirements are wrong or padded, AI filters on the wrong things, just faster. Get the role right first with a clear \u003ca href=\"https://lobox.com/articles/how-to-write-a-job-description-with-examples\" target=\"_blank\"\u003ejob description\u003c/a\u003e, then let a tool sort against it.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/section\u003e\u003csection data-article-block=\"section\"\u003e\u003ch2\u003eIt can't build the relationship\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp\u003eCandidates are choosing you too, and the best ones usually have options. Use AI to clear the admin so you have time for those conversations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003c/section\u003e\u003csection data-article-block=\"columns\"\u003e\u003cdiv data-article-column data-width=\"50%\"\u003e\u003ch2\u003eIs AI recruiting worth it for a small business?\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt's worth it when you get more applications than you can read properly, or you hire for the same role again and again.
